opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the distinction is actually less sharp than people assume, and that's part of the point. Statistical similarity, the way most deep learning uses it, is a similarity between surface representations. Two inputs are close in embedding space, so the network treats them alike. That's useful, but it's shallow: you get interpolation, not structure. The model doesn't know *why* two things are similar, or which parts of one correspond to which parts of the other.

Analogical reasoning is about mapping structure. When you say an atom is like a solar system, you're not saying electrons look like planets. You're saying the *relations* carry over: something orbits something else, held by an attractive force. Classic symbolic AI could do that kind of structure mapping, but it was brittle. It couldn't handle degrees of similarity, and it didn't learn.

What TensorLogic does is put both in the same language. Relations are tensors, rules are tensor equations, and you can embed objects and relations in a vector space. When you reason in embedding space, there's essentially a temperature parameter. At zero temperature you get pure deduction: the rule applies exactly to the things it's about, no hallucinations, just logic. As you raise the temperature, the rule starts to apply to things that are *similar* to what it was stated for. That's analogy. But the similarity isn't just "these vectors are close"; it's propagating through the structure of the rules. You're borrowing inferences along relational pathways, not just copying labels from nearest neighbors.

So the way I'd put it: statistical similarity says "this looks like that." Analogical reasoning in TensorLogic says "this plays the same role as that in a structure, so the conclusions that hold there probably hold here, with some confidence." And because it's one formalism, you can dial between the two and see exactly what the system is doing, which you can't do with a transformer, where it's all mixed together and opaque.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, that's really the crux of it, isn't it? Because on the surface they can look the same. Statistical similarity is what you get from embeddings: you take two things, map them into a vector space, and measure the distance. Two words are similar because they occur in similar contexts, two images are similar because they activate similar features. It's a scalar. It's a number between zero and one, and once you have it, you've thrown away everything about why they're similar.

Analogy is a different beast. Analogy is structural. When you say the atom is like the solar system, you're not saying the atom looks like the solar system. You're saying there's a mapping: the nucleus plays the role of the sun, the electrons play the role of the planets, and the relation "orbits" carries over. The similarity is in the relations, not in the objects. Gentner called this structure mapping, and it's been the standard account in cognitive science for forty years. And the key thing is that once you have that mapping, you can transfer inferences. If planets further out move more slowly, maybe electrons further out do too. You get to make predictions in the target domain that you never observed there, because you're borrowing the structure of the source.

Now, what TensorLogic lets you do is have both in one framework. The reason is that in TensorLogic a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same thing. A rule like "grandparent of X and Z if parent of X and Y and parent of Y and Z" is literally a tensor contraction over the shared index Y. So relations are tensors, objects are indices into those tensors, and inference is tensor algebra. When you do that, you can do things in the embedding space that are purely statistical, which is what a transformer does, but you can also do things over the relational structure, which is what an analogy needs. The structure mapping becomes a question of which tensors align with which, and under what correspondence of indices the contractions still go through. That's a well-defined operation, not a vibe.

And here's the part I think people miss. In an ordinary neural network, if two things are similar, you have no way of asking in what respect. The network just says, these two are close. In TensorLogic you can ask: close along which relation? Close because they both participate in the same pattern of predicates? That's the difference between "these look alike" and "these are the same kind of thing for this purpose." The first is correlation. The second is the beginning of reasoning. And I'd argue most of what we call generalization in humans is the second kind, and most of what we're getting from large language models today is still mostly the first kind, with the second kind leaking in by accident when the statistics happen to line up with the structure.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish them by asking what is being matched. Statistical similarity typically says that two things have similar features, or that their vectors are close in some representation. Analogy asks whether the relationships in one situation correspond to the relationships in another. The objects themselves might look very different.

Take the analogy between a solar system and an atom. What makes that analogy interesting is a proposed correspondence between roles and relationships, not that a planet looks like an electron. And the analogy has limits: matching some structure doesn’t mean that every property transfers.

The idea with TensorLogic is to put representations and logical relationships into a common tensor framework. So you can use learned similarity to suggest a correspondence, while expressing the relational constraints that make that correspondence meaningful. The important distinction isn’t tensors versus symbols. It’s resemblance versus a mapping of structure that supports an inference.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, statistical similarity asks, “Do these things have similar features?” Analogy asks, “Do these things have a similar structure?” Two things can look very different and still participate in the same pattern of relationships.

Take the analogy between the solar system and an atom. The useful correspondence isn’t that an electron looks like a planet. It’s the relationship between the elements of each system. And, of course, that analogy has limits—you don’t want to transfer every property of planets to electrons.

The idea in TensorLogic is to bring relational structure and numerical representations into the same framework. Similarity can help you propose a correspondence, but the relationships constrain whether that correspondence makes sense and what you can infer from it. So statistical similarity can be an ingredient in analogy. The additional step is finding a mapping that preserves relevant structure and lets you draw a new inference.
